title: Whither thou goest (Ruth 1)
hook: a widowed Moabite refuses to leave her mother-in-law: your people shall be my people

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samson's last prayer in the temple of Dagon, and your line was remember me, just this once. Who did you ask for help, and how plain was the sentence? Day seven hundred seven.

Three widows on a road out of Moab. The book of Ruth opens "in the days when the judges ruled," the same troubled years we've just walked through, and it opens small. A famine in Bethlehem. A man named Elimelech takes his wife Naomi and their two sons to Moab to find food. He dies there. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. About ten years go by, and both sons die too. Now Naomi hears that the LORD has given his people bread again, and she starts for home with her two daughters-in-law. Somewhere on that road she stops and turns around. Go back, she tells them. Each of you, go back to your mother's house. I have nothing left to give you.
screen: `GO BACK, EACH TO YOUR MOTHER'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: They weep. Then the two women choose differently, and the text puts it in one short verse: "Orpah kissed her mother in law; but Ruth clave unto her." Notice that Orpah isn't blamed. She does what Naomi asked, and kisses her goodbye. The story blames neither woman. It simply stays with the harder choice. Clave is the old past tense of cleave, to hold fast. The King James uses the same word in Genesis, where a man shall leave his father and mother "and shall cleave unto his wife." Here it's a daughter-in-law holding on to a mother-in-law, a Moabite to an Israelite, a young widow to an old one with nothing to offer. Naomi tries once more, and Ruth answers with the lines this day is named for: "Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Listen to how it climbs. The road. The bed. The people. God. Then she keeps going, all the way down: where you die, I'll die, and there I'll be buried. She isn't promising a trip. She's promising a whole life, and a grave in a foreign country. The text says that when Naomi saw she was steadfastly minded, she stopped arguing. Then a detail that's easy to miss. When the two of them reach Bethlehem and the town comes out to look, Naomi says, "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me." And: "I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty." Empty. Ruth is standing right beside her. Some readers hear a grief so deep it doesn't count her. Ruth stays anyway. The chapter ends at the start of barley harvest, which matters tomorrow.
screen: `ORPAH KISSED HER; RUTH CLAVE UNTO HER.`
`THE ROAD, THE BED, THE PEOPLE, GOD.`
`CALL ME MARA. I CAME HOME EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay with someone who's lost much. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who is carrying a loss right now: a death, a divorce, a job, their health. Maybe they're bitter. Maybe they've stopped noticing who's still around. Don't wait for them to thank you. Nobody thanks Ruth here. Just hold them in mind for these two minutes, and decide one way you'll stay close this week. A call. A meal. Sitting with them. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Naomi. The widowed mother-in-law Ruth refused to leave, who later renamed herself Mara, bitter, after losing everything and returning to Bethlehem empty.
Your line: where you go, I go. Today, show up for the person you named, even in a small way, without needing them to notice. Day seven hundred seven.

howItsDone: Christians read Ruth's vow as a picture of faithful love that crosses family, nation and grief, a love that holds on when the other person has stopped hoping.

fork.setup: you're Ruth. your husband is dead. your mother-in-law, old and poor, tells you to go back to your mother's house in Moab. what do you do?
options: kiss her goodbye and go home.
refuse: whither thou goest, I will go.
go with her as far as the border, then decide.
fork.reveal: Ruth clave unto her, and vowed to go, lodge, live, worship, die and be buried where Naomi did (Ruth 1:16–17).

original.note: Hebrew: clave, held fast. Ruth 1:14 says Ruth clave unto Naomi.

trapdoor: what you thought: a romantic line between two lovers.
what it means: a young Moabite widow's vow to her widowed Israelite mother-in-law, on the road home.
what a scholar hears: Ruth 1:14's clave (davqah), the verb of holding fast that Genesis 2:24 uses for a man cleaving to his wife.
recall: devoted to God, taken out of use

notes: 'About ten years' is from Ruth 1:4. The arrival at the beginning of barley harvest is Ruth 1:22.
Ruth 1:17 and 1:18 ('stedfastly minded') are paraphrased, not quoted.

Claim that Ruth 1:14 (דָּבְקָה) and Genesis 2:24 (וְדָבַק) share the verb dabaq, and that the KJV renders both 'clave/cleave': please confirm. Pointing and pronunciation of דָּבְקָה (dav-KAH) to check.
Orpah is presented without blame, matching the text; some later Jewish and Christian readings are harsher on her, deliberately left out.
'Naomi is too deep in grief to count her' is an interpretive reading, attributed to 'some readers'.
Editor 2: cut 'across the Jordan' from the hook; Ruth 1:1 says only that the family went to sojourn in the country of Moab.
Audit: "two good choices" (a narrator verdict the text does not give) now "the story blames neither woman".

Editor: the reading of Naomi's 'empty' is now explicitly attributed to some readers (it was stated as fact); 'Ruth wasn't thanked' narrowed to 'nobody in this chapter thanks Ruth'; stock opener 'the detail some readers can't get past' replaced.
